Ord. No. 13984. Taking Additional Steps To Address the National Emergency With Respect to Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities\nEx. Ord. No. 13984, Jan. 19, 2021, 86 F.R. 6837, provided:\nBy the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, including the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.) (NEA), and section 301 of title 3, United States Code:\nI, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, find that additional steps must be taken to deal with the national emergency related to significant malicious cyber-enabled activities declared in Executive Order 13694 of April 1, 2015 (Blocking the Property of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities), as amended [50 U.S.C. 1701 note], to address the use of United States Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) products by foreign malicious cyber actors. IaaS products provide persons the ability to run software and store data on servers offered for rent or lease without responsibility for the maintenance and operating costs of those servers. Foreign malicious cyber actors aim to harm the United States economy through the theft of intellectual property and sensitive data and to threaten national security by targeting United States critical infrastructure for malicious cyber-enabled activities. Foreign actors use United States IaaS products for a variety of tasks in carrying out malicious cyber-enabled activities, which makes it extremely difficult for United States officials to track and obtain information through legal process before these foreign actors transition to replacement infrastructure and destroy evidence of their prior activities; foreign resellers of United States IaaS products make it easier for foreign actors to access these products and evade detection. This order provides authority to impose record-keeping obligations with respect to foreign transactions. To address these threats, to deter foreign malicious cyber actors’ use of United States IaaS products, and to assist in the investigation of transactions involving foreign malicious cyber actors, the United States must ensure that providers offering United States IaaS products verify the identity of persons obtaining an IaaS account (“Account”) for the provision of these products and maintain records of those transactions. In appropriate circumstances, to further protect against malicious cyber-enabled activities, the United States must also limit certain foreign actors’ access to United States IaaS products. Further, the United States must encourage more robust cooperation among United States IaaS providers, including by increasing voluntary information sharing, to bolster efforts to thwart the actions of foreign malicious cyber actors.\nAccordingly, I hereby order:","sections_touched":["section 3502","sections 272","section wording lead; chronology does not decide legal effect.","provision_text":"Section 1. Policy. It is the policy of the United States to restrict access by countries of concern to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data when such access would pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. At the same time, the United States continues to support open, global, interoperable, reliable, and secure flows of data across borders, as well as maintaining vital consumer, economic, scientific, and trade relationships that the United States has with other countries.\n\nThe continuing effort by countries of concern to access Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data threatens the national security and foreign policy of the United States. Such countries' governments may seek to access and use sensitive personal data in a manner that is not in accordance with democratic values, safeguards for privacy, and other human rights and freedoms. Such countries' approach stands in sharp contrast to the practices of democracies with respect to sensitive personal data and principles reflected in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development Declaration on Government Access to Personal Data Held by Private Sector Entities. Unrestricted transfers of Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data to such countries of concern may therefore enable them to exploit such data for a variety of nefarious purposes, including to engage in malicious cyber-enabled activities. Countries of concern can use their access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data to track and build profiles on United States individuals, including Federal employees and contractors, for illicit purposes, including blackmail and espionage. Access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data by countries of concern through data brokerages, third-party vendor agreements, employment agreements, investment agreements, or other such arrangements poses particular and unacceptable risks to our national security given that these arrangements often can provide countries of concern with direct and unfettered access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data. Countries of concern can use access to United States persons' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data to collect information on activists, academics, journalists, dissidents, political figures, or members of non-governmental organizations or marginalized communities in order to intimidate such persons; curb dissent or political opposition; otherwise limit freedoms of expression, peaceful assembly, or association; or enable other forms of suppression of civil liberties.\n\nThis risk of access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data is not limited to direct access by countries of concern. Entities owned by, and entities or individuals controlled by or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of, a country of concern may enable the government of a country of concern to indirectly access such data. For example, a country of concern may have cyber, national security, or intelligence laws that, without sufficient legal safeguards, obligate such entities and individuals to provide that country's intelligence services access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data.\n\nThese risks may be exacerbated when countries of concern use bulk sensitive personal data to develop AI capabilities and algorithms that, in turn, enable the use of large datasets in increasingly sophisticated and effective ways to the detriment of United States national security. Countries of concern can use AI to target United States persons for espionage or blackmail by, for example, recognizing patterns across multiple unrelated datasets to identify potential individuals whose links to the Federal Government would be otherwise obscured in a single dataset.\n\nWhile aspects of this threat have been addressed in previous executive actions, such as Executive Order 13694 of April 1, 2015 (Blocking the Property of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities), as amended, additional steps need to be taken to address this threat.\n\nAt the same time, the United States is committed to promoting an open, global, interoperable, reliable, and secure Internet; protecting human rights online and offline; supporting a vibrant, global economy by promoting cross-border data flows required to enable international commerce and trade; and facilitating open investment. To ensure that the United States continues to meet these important policy objectives, this order does not authorize the imposition of generalized data localization requirements to store Americans' bulk sensitive personal data or United States Government-related data within the United States or to locate computing facilities used to process Americans' bulk sensitive personal data or United States Government-related data within the United States. This order also does not broadly prohibit United States persons from conducting commercial transactions, including exchanging financial and other data as part of the sale of commercial goods and services, with entities and individuals located in or subject to the control, direction, or jurisdiction of countries of concern, or impose measures aimed at a broader decoupling of the substantial consumer, economic, scientific, and trade relationships that the United States has with other countries. In addition, my Administration has made commitments to increase public access to the results of taxpayer-funded scientific research, the sharing and interoperability of electronic health information, and patient access to their data. The national security restrictions established in this order are specific, carefully calibrated actions to minimize the risks associated with access to bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data by countries of concern while minimizing disruption to commercial activity. This order shall be implemented consistent with these policy objectives, including by tailoring any regulations issued and actions taken pursuant to this order to address the national security threat posed by access to Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data by countries of concern.","sections_touched":["Section 1"],"signing_date":"2024-02-28","source":{"acceptable_as_original":false,"archival_id":"app:node/370086","filing_date":null,"grade":"mirror_transcription","instrument_id":"EO:14117","location_confidence":"medium","location_verified":false,"page_or_item":"Executive Order 14117—Preventing Access to Americans' Bulk Sensitive Personal Data and United States Government-Related Data by Countries of Concern; February 28, 2024; APP node 370086; common-crawl capture 2025-11-11T06:34:11Z","requires_page_check":true,"sha256":"006998d512c2660d9d273ebae3153a2bb45783cfa33dcf72f49872463356fffc","signing_date":"2024-02-28","text_path":"jobs/app-executive-orders/output/texts/executive-order-14117-preventing-access-americans-bulk-sensitive-personal-data-and-united.txt","text_sha256":"5f31428cefaffbe43a0c7eb7d02dd5324da239f14ad870e88d753606a7b5aa52","url":"https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/executive-order-14117-preventing-access-americans-bulk-sensitive-personal-data-and-united"},"verb":"transfer"},{"actor_id":"EO:14117","char_end":9775,"char_start":2644,"confidence":"medium","how_named":"direct","id":"CHAIN:EO:13694#26","notes":"Change wording lead; chronology does not decide legal effect.","provision_text":"Section 1. Policy. It is the policy of the United States to restrict access \nby countries of concern to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and \nUnited States Government-related data when such access would pose an \nunacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. At the same \ntime, the United States continues to support open, global, interoperable, \nreliable, and secure flows of data across borders, as well as maintaining \nvital consumer, economic, scientific, and trade relationships that the United \nStates has with other countries. \nThe continuing effort by countries of concern to access Americans’ bulk \nsensitive personal data and United States Government-related data threatens \nthe national security and foreign policy of the United States. Such countries’ \ngovernments may seek to access and use sensitive personal data in a manner \nVerDate Sep<11>2014 22:57 Feb 29, 2024 Jkt 262001 PO 00000 Frm 00003 Fmt 4705 Sfmt 4790 E:\\FR\\FM\\01MRE0.SGM 01MRE0ddrumheller on DSK120RN23PROD with PRESDOC-E0\n=== PDF page 2 of 10 ===\n15422 Federal Register / Vol. 89, No. 42 / Friday, March 1, 2024 / Presidential Documents \nthat is not in accordance with democratic values, safeguards for privacy, \nand other human rights and freedoms. Such countries’ approach stands \nin sharp contrast to the practices of democracies with respect to sensitive \npersonal data and principles reflected in the Organisation for Economic \nCo-operation and Development Declaration on Government Access to Per-\nsonal Data Held by Private Sector Entities. Unrestricted transfers of Ameri-\ncans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related \ndata to such countries of concern may therefore enable them to exploit \nsuch data for a variety of nefarious purposes, including to engage in malicious \ncyber-enabled activities. Countries of concern can use their access to Ameri-\ncans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related \ndata to track and build profiles on United States individuals, including \nFederal employees and contractors, for illicit purposes, including blackmail \nand espionage. Access to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United \nStates Government-related data by countries of concern through data \nbrokerages, third-party vendor agreements, employment agreements, invest-\nment agreements, or other such arrangements poses particular and unaccept-\nable risks to our national security given that these arrangements often can \nprovide countries of concern with direct and unfettered access to Americans’ \nbulk sensitive personal data. Countries of concern can use access to United \nStates persons’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government- \nrelated data to collect information on activists, academics, journalists, dis-\nsidents, political figures, or members of non-governmental organizations or \nmarginalized communities in order to intimidate such persons; curb dissent \nor political opposition; otherwise limit freedoms of expression, peaceful \nassembly, or association; or enable other forms of suppression of civil lib-\nerties. \nThis risk of access to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United \nStates Government-related data is not limited to direct access by countries \nof concern. Entities owned by, and entities or individuals controlled by \nor subject to the jurisdiction or direction of, a country of concern may \nenable the government of a country of concern to indirectly access such \ndata. For example, a country of concern may have cyber, national security, \nor intelligence laws that, without sufficient legal safeguards, obligate such \nentities and individuals to provide that country’s intelligence services access \nto Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government- \nrelated data. \nThese risks may be exacerbated when countries of concern use bulk sensitive \npersonal data to develop AI capabilities and algorithms that, in turn, enable \nthe use of large datasets in increasingly sophisticated and effective ways \nto the detriment of United States national security. sense of Congress that—\n“(1)\n the Russian Federation bears responsibility for the financial burden of the reconstruction of Ukraine and for countless other costs associated with the illegal invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation that began on February 24, 2022;\n“(2)\n the most effective ways to provide compensation for the damages caused by the Russian Federation’s internationally wrongful acts should be assessed by an international mechanism charged with determining compensation and providing assistance to Ukraine;\n“(3)\n at least since November 2022 the Russian Federation has been on notice of its opportunity to comply with its international obligations, including to make full compensation for injury, or, by agreement with Ukraine, to authorize an international mechanism to resolve issues regarding compensation to Ukraine;\n“(4)\n the Russian Federation can, by negotiated agreement, participate in any international process to assess the damages caused by the Russian Federation’s internationally wrongful acts and make funds available to compensate for these damages, and if it fails to do so, the United States and other countries should explore all avenues for ensuring compensation to Ukraine;\n“(5)\n the President should lead robust engagement on all bilateral and multilateral aspects of the response by the United States to acts by the Russian Federation that undermine the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine, including on any policy coordination and alignment regarding the repurposing or ordered transfer of Russian sovereign assets in the context of determining compensation and providing assistance to Ukraine;\n“(6)\n as part of the robust engagement on bilateral and multilateral responses to acts by the Russian Federation that undermine the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine, the President should endeavor to facilitate creation of, and United States participation in, an international mechanism regarding the repurposing or seizure of sovereign assets of the Russian Federation for the benefit of Ukraine.[;]\n“(7)\n the repurposing of Russian sovereign assets is in the national interests of the United States and consistent with United States and international law;\n“(8)\n the United States should work with international allies and partners on the repurposing of Russian sovereign assets as part of a coordinated, multilateral effort, including with G7 countries and other countries in which Russian sovereign assets are located; and\n“(9)\n any effort by the United States to confiscate and repurpose Russian sovereign assets should be undertaken alongside international allies and partners as part of a coordinated, multilateral effort, including with G7 countries, the European Union, Australia, and other countries in which Russian sovereign assets are located.\n“SEC. 103."},{"char_end":43610,"char_start":35783,"text":"E, title LV, § 5590, Dec. 23, 2022, 136 Stat. 3380, provided that:\n“(a)\n Identification.—\nNot later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this Act [Dec. 23, 2022], and periodically as necessary thereafter, the President—\n“(1)\n shall submit to Congress a report identifying foreign persons that knowingly participated in a significant transaction—\n“(A)\n for the sale, supply, or transfer (including transportation) of gold, directly or indirectly, to or from the Russian Federation or the Government of the Russian Federation, including from reserves of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation held outside the Russian Federation; or\n“(B)\n that otherwise involved gold in which the Government of the Russian Federation had any interest; and\n“(2)\n shall impose the sanctions described in subsection (b)(1) with respect to each such person; and\n“(3)\n may impose the sanctions described in subsection (b)(2) with respect to any such person that is an alien.\n“(b)\n Sanctions Described.—\nThe sanctions described in this subsection are the following:\n“(1)\n Blocking of property.—\nThe exercise of all powers granted to the President by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) to the extent necessary to block and prohibit all transactions in all property and interests in property of a foreign person identified in the report required by subsection (a)(1) if such property and interests in property are in the United States, come within the United States, or are or come within the possession or control of a United States person.\n“(2)\n Ineligibility for visas, admission, or parole.—\n“(A)\n Visas, admission, or parole.—\nAn alien described in subsection (a)(1) is—\n“(i)\n inadmissible to the United States;\n“(ii)\n ineligible to receive a visa or other documentation to enter the United States; and\n“(iii)\n otherwise ineligible to be admitted or paroled into the United States or to receive any other benefit under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.).\n“(B)\n Current visas revoked.—\n“(i)\n In general.—\nThe issuing consular officer, the Secretary of State, or the Secretary of Homeland Security (or a designee of one of such Secretaries) shall, in accordance with section 221(i) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1201(i)), revoke any visa or other entry documentation issued to an alien described in subsection (a)(1).\n“(ii)\n Immediate effect.—\nThe revocation under clause (i) of a visa or other entry documentation issued to an alien shall—\n     “(I)\n take effect immediately; and\n     “(II)\n automatically cancel any other valid visa or entry documentation that is in the alien’s possession.\n“(c)\n Implementation; Penalties.—\n“(1)\n Implementation.—\nThe President may exercise all authorities provided under sections 203 and 205 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1702 and 1704) to carry out this section.\n“(2)\n Penalties.—\nA person that violates, attempts to violate, conspires to violate, or causes a violation of this section or any regulation, license, or order issued to carry out this section shall be subject to the penalties set forth in subsections (b) and (c) of section 206 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1705) to the same extent as a person that commits an unlawful act described in subsection (a) of that section.\n“(d)\n National Interest Waiver.—\nThe President may waive the imposition of sanctions under this section with respect to a person if the President—\n“(1)\n determines that such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States; and\n“(2)\n submits to Congress a notification of the waiver and the reasons for the waiver.\n“(e)\n Termination.—\n“(1)\n In general.—\nExcept as provided in paragraph (2), the requirement to impose sanctions under this section, and any sanctions imposed under this section, shall terminate on the earlier of—\n“(A)\n the date that is 3 years after the date of the enactment of this Act; or\n“(B)\n the date that is 30 days after the date on which the President certifies to Congress that—\n“(i)\n the Government of the Russian Federation has ceased its destabilizing activities with respect to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine; and\n“(ii)\n such termination in the national interests of the United States.\n“(2)\n Transition rules.—\n“(A)\n Continuation of certain authorities.—\nAny authorities exercised before the termination date under paragraph (1) to impose sanctions with respect to a foreign person under this section may continue to be exercised on and after that date if the President determines that the continuation of those authorities is in the national interests of the United States.\n“(B)\n Application to ongoing investigations.—\nThe termination date under paragraph (1) shall not apply to any investigation of a civil or criminal violation of this section or any regulation, license, or order issued to carry out this section, or the imposition of a civil or criminal penalty for such a violation, if—\n“(i)\n the violation occurred before the termination date; or\n“(ii)\n the person involved in the violation continues to be subject to sanctions pursuant to subparagraph (A).\n“(f)\n Exceptions.—\n“(1)\n Exceptions for authorized intelligence and law enforcement and national security activities.—\nThis section shall not apply with respect to activities subject to the reporting requirements under title V of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 3091 et seq.) or any authorized intelligence, law enforcement, or national security activities of the United States.\n“(2)\n Exception to comply with international agreements.—\nSanctions under subsection (b)(2) may not apply with respect to the admission of an alien to the United States if such admission is necessary to comply with the obligations of the United States under the Agreement regarding the Headquarters of the United Nations, signed at Lake Success June 26, 1947, and entered into force November 21, 1947, between the United Nations and the United States, or the Convention on Consular Relations, done at Vienna April 24, 1963, and entered into force March 19, 1967, or other international obligations.\n“(3)\n Humanitarian exemption.—\nThe President shall not impose sanctions under this section with respect to any person for conducting or facilitating a transaction for the sale of agricultural commodities, food, medicine, or medical devices or for the provision of humanitarian assistance.\n“(4)\n Exception relating to importation of goods.—\n“(A)\n In general.—\nThe requirement or authority to impose sanctions under this section shall not include the authority or a requirement to impose sanctions on the importation of goods.\n“(B)\n Good defined.—\nIn this paragraph, the term ‘good’ means any article, natural or manmade substance, material, supply, or manufactured product, including inspection and test equipment, and excluding technical data.\n“(g)\n Definitions.—\nIn this section:\n“(1)\n The terms ‘admission’, ‘admitted’, ‘alien’, and ‘lawfully admitted for permanent residence’ have the meanings given those terms in section 101 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101).\n“(2)\n The term ‘foreign person’ means an individual or entity that is not a United States person.\n“(3)\n The term ‘knowingly’, with respect to conduct, a circumstance, or a result, means that a person has actual knowledge, or should have known, of the conduct, the circumstance, or the result.\n“(4)\n The term ‘United States person’ means—\n“(A)\n a United States citizen or an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence to the United States;\n“(B)\n an entity organized under the laws of the United States or any jurisdiction within the United States, including a foreign branch of such an entity; or\n“(C)\n any person in the United States.”\nExecutive Documents\nEx."},{"char_end":60481,"char_start":60207,"text":"I therefore determine that for these measures to be effective in addressing the national emergencies declared in Executive Orders 13660 and 13694, there need be no prior notice of an action taken pursuant to this order with respect to such property or interests in property."}],"exceptions_text":["provided Indirect parent membership is an unconfirmed lead.","provision_label":"Sec. 6.","reaches_target_via":"EO:13694 as amended","savings_phrases":[],"scope":"partial","signing_date":"2021-01-19","target_id":"EO:13757","verb":"amend"}
  Text: [Te179c7b754900e626da5fa0d](#te179c7b754900e626da5fa0d); absolute characters 19114–19214
- **ACT:EO:13757>EO:14110**; S27a52a98d3101e20dd98a07c; {"actor_id":"EO:14110","char_end":31181,"char_start":29642,"confidence":"medium","effective_class":"unknown","effective_date":null,"effective_wording":[{"char_end":4059,"char_start":3864,"text":"Finally, my Administration will help develop effective \nlabeling and content provenance mechanisms, so that Americans are able \nto determine when content is generated using AI and when it is not."},{"char_end":11920,"char_start":11733,"text":"Effective leader-\nship also means pioneering those systems and safeguards needed to deploy \ntechnology responsibly—and building and promoting those safeguards with \nthe rest of the world."},{"char_end":17131,"char_start":16879,"text":"(l) The term ‘‘Federal law enforcement agency’’ has the meaning set forth \nin section 21(a) of Executive Order 14074 of May 25, 2022 (Advancing \nEffective, Accountable Policing and Criminal Justice Practices To Enhance \nPublic Trust and Public Safety)."},{"char_end":27603,"char_start":26208,"text":"(a) Within 90 days of the date of this \norder, to ensure and verify the continuous availability of safe, reliable, \nand effective AI in accordance with the Defense Production Act, as amended, \n50 U.S.C. 4501 et seq., including for the national defense and the protection \nof critical infrastructure, the Secretary of Commerce shall require: \n(i) Companies developing or demonstrating an intent to develop potential \ndual-use foundation models to provide the Federal Government, on an \nongoing basis, with information, reports, or records regarding the following: \n(A) any ongoing or planned activities related to training, developing, \nor producing dual-use foundation models, including the physical and \ncybersecurity protections taken to assure the integrity of that training \nprocess against sophisticated threats; \n(B) the ownership and possession of the model weights of any dual- \nuse foundation models, and the physical and cybersecurity measures taken \nto protect those model weights; and \n(C) the results of any developed dual-use foundation model’s perform-\nance in relevant AI red-team testing based on guidance developed by \nNIST pursuant to subsection 4.1(a)(ii) of this section, and a description \nof any associated measures the company has taken to meet safety objectives, \nsuch as mitigations to improve performance on these red-team tests and \nstrengthen overall model security."},{"char_end":48376,"char_start":47189,"text":"(ii) Within 180 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of Commerce, \nacting through the Director of NIST, in coordination with the Director \nVerDate Sep<11>2014 23:02 Oct 31, 2023 Jkt 262001 PO 00000 Frm 00013 Fmt 4705 Sfmt 4790 E:\\FR\\FM\\01NOE0.SGM 01NOE0ddrumheller on DSK120RN23PROD with PRESDOC-E0\n=== PDF page 12 of 36 ===\n75202 Federal Register / Vol. 88, No. 210 / Wednesday, November 1, 2023 / Presidential Documents \nof OSTP, and in consultation with the Secretary of State, the Secretary \nof HHS, and the heads of other relevant agencies as the Secretary of \nCommerce may deem appropriate, shall initiate an effort to engage with \nindustry and relevant stakeholders, informed by the framework developed \nunder subsection 4.4(b)(i) of this section, to develop and refine for possible \nuse by synthetic nucleic acid sequence providers: \n(A) specifications for effective nucleic acid synthesis procurement screen-\ning; \n(B) best practices, including security and access controls, for managing \nsequence-of-concern databases to support such screening; \n(C) technical implementation guides for effective screening; and \n(D) conformity-assessment best practices and mechanisms."},{"char_end":50295,"char_start":49068,"text":"(iv) In order to facilitate effective implementation of the measures described \nin subsections 4.4(b)(i)–(iii) of this section, the Secretary of Homeland \nSecurity, in consultation with the heads of other relevant agencies as \nthe Secretary of Homeland Security may deem appropriate, shall: \n(A) within 180 days of the establishment of the framework pursuant \nto subsection 4.4(b)(i) of this section, develop a framework to conduct \nstructured evaluation and stress testing of nucleic acid synthesis procure-\nment screening, including the systems developed in accordance with sub-\nsections 4.4(b)(i)–(ii) of this section and implemented by providers of \nsynthetic nucleic acid sequences; and \n(B) following development of the framework pursuant to subsection \n4.4(b)(iv)(A) of this section, submit an annual report to the Assistant \nto the President for National Security Affairs, the Director of the Office \nof Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy, and the Director of OSTP \non any results of the activities conducted pursuant to subsection \n4.4(b)(iv)(A) of this section, including recommendations, if any, on how \nto strengthen nucleic acid synthesis procurement screening, including cus-\ntomer screening systems. \n4.5."},{"char_end":76011,"char_start":75830,"text":"The report shall include a discussion of issues that may hinder the effective \nuse of AI in research and practices needed to ensure that AI is used respon-\nsibly for research. \n5.3."},{"char_end":112098,"char_start":111612,"text":"The RFI shall seek \nfeedback regarding how privacy impact assessments may be more effective \nat mitigating privacy risks, including those that are further exacerbated \nby AI; and \n(iv) take such steps as are necessary and appropriate, consistent with \napplicable law, to support and advance the near-term actions and long- \nterm strategy identified through the RFI process, including issuing new \nor updated guidance or RFIs or consulting other agencies or the Federal \nPrivacy Council."},{"char_end":115721,"char_start":115253,"text":"(b) To provide guidance on Federal Government use of AI, within 150 \ndays of the date of this order and updated periodically thereafter, the Director \nof OMB, in coordination with the Director of OSTP, and in consultation \nwith the interagency council established in subsection 10.1(a) of this section, \nshall issue guidance to agencies to strengthen the effective and appropriate \nuse of AI, advance AI innovation, and manage risks from AI in the Federal \nGovernment."}],"exceptions_text":[],"filing_date":null,"id":"ACT:EO:13757>EO:14110","names_target":false,"notes":"Machine lead only;   Text: [Tf361bad41af4aae4ecbf6cf6](#tf361bad41af4aae4ecbf6cf6); absolute characters 115253–115721
- **ACT:EO:13757>EO:14117**; Sf9b69c68a0ae5157c023bb73; {"actor_id":"EO:14117","char_end":10384,"char_start":3253,"confidence":"medium","effective_class":"unknown","effective_date":null,"effective_wording":[{"char_end":7344,"char_start":7060,"text":"These risks may be exacerbated when countries of concern use bulk sensitive \npersonal data to develop AI capabilities and algorithms that, in turn, enable \nthe use of large datasets in increasingly sophisticated and effective ways \nto the detriment of United States national security."},{"char_end":12411,"char_start":10434,"text":"(a) To assist in addressing \nthe national emergency described in this order, the Attorney General, in \ncoordination with the Secretary of Homeland Security and in consultation \nwith the heads of relevant agencies, shall issue, subject to public notice \nand comment, regulations that prohibit or otherwise restrict United States \npersons from engaging in any acquisition, holding, use, transfer, transpor-\ntation, or exportation of, or dealing in, any property in which a foreign \ncountry or national thereof has any interest (transaction), where the trans-\naction: \n(i) involves bulk sensitive personal data or United States Government- \nrelated data, as further defined by regulations issued by the Attorney \nGeneral pursuant to this section; \n(ii) is a member of a class of transactions that has been determined \nby the Attorney General, in regulations issued by the Attorney General \npursuant to this section, to pose an unacceptable risk to the national \nsecurity of the United States because the transactions may enable countries \nof concern or covered persons to access bulk sensitive personal data \nor United States Government-related data in a manner that contributes \nto the national emergency described in this order; \n(iii) was initiated, is pending, or will be completed after the effective \ndate of the regulations issued by the Attorney General pursuant to this \nsection; \n(iv) does not qualify for an exemption provided in, or is not authorized \nby a license issued pursuant to, the regulations issued by the Attorney \nGeneral pursuant to this section; and \n(v) is not, as defined by regulations issued by the Attorney General pursuant \nto this section, ordinarily incident to and part of the provision of financial \nservices, including banking, capital markets, and financial insurance serv-\nices, or required for compliance with any Federal statutory or regulatory \nrequirements, including any regulations, guidance, or orders implementing \nthose requirements."}],"exceptions_text":[],"filing_date":null,"id":"ACT:EO:13757>EO:14117","names_target":false,"notes":"Machine lead only; does not decide legal effect.","provision_text":"(i)\n full compensation has been made to Ukraine for harms resulting from the invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation;\n“(ii)\n the Russian Federation is participating in a bona fide international mechanism that, by agreement, will discharge the obligations of the Russian Federation to compensate Ukraine for all amounts determined to be owed to Ukraine; or\n“(iii)\n the Russian Federation’s obligation to compensate Ukraine for the damage caused by the Russian Federation’s aggression has been resolved pursuant to an agreement between the Russian Federation and the Government of Ukraine.\n“SEC. 105.\n INTERNATIONAL MECHANISM TO USE RUSSIAN SOVEREIGN ASSETS AND RUSSIAN AGGRESSOR STATE SOVEREIGN ASSETS TO PROVIDE FOR THE RECONSTRUCTION OF UKRAINE.\n“(a)\n In General.—\nThe President shall take such actions as the President determines appropriate to coordinate with the G7, the European Union, Australia, and other partners and allies of the United States regarding the disposition of immobilized Russian aggressor state sovereign assets, including seeking to establish an international mechanism with foreign partners, including Ukraine, the G7, the European Union, Australia, and other partners and allies of the United States, for the purpose of assisting Ukraine, which may include the establishment of an international fund to be known as the ‘Ukraine Compensation Fund’, that may receive and use assets in the Ukraine Support Fund established under section 104(c) [probably should be “section 104(d)”] and contributions from foreign partners that have also frozen or seized Russian aggressor state sovereign assets to assist Ukraine, including by—\n“(1)\n supporting a register of damage to serve as a record of evidence and for assessment of the financially assessable damages to Ukraine resulting from the invasions of Ukraine by the Russian Federation and operations or actions in support thereof;\n“(2)\n establishing a mechanism to compensate Ukraine for damages caused by Russia’s internationally wrongful acts connected with the invasions of Ukraine;\n“(3)\n ensuring distribution of those assets or the proceeds of those assets based on determinations under that mechanism; and\n“(4)\n taking such other actions as may be necessary to carry out this section.\n“(b)\n Authorization for Deposit in the Ukraine Compensation Fund.—\nUpon the President reaching an agreement or arrangement to establish a common international mechanism pursuant to subsection (a) or at any time thereafter, the Secretary of State may, pursuant to the authority conferred by and subject to the limitations described in section 104(f) [probably should be “section 104(g)”] and subject to the limitations described in subsection (e), transfer funds from the Ukraine Support Fund established under section 104(d) to a fund or mechanism established consistent with subsection (a).\n“(c)\n Notification.—\nThe President shall notify the appropriate congressional committees not later than 30 days after entering into any new bilateral or multilateral agreement or arrangement under subsection (a).\n“(d)\n Good Governance.—\nThe Secretary of State, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, shall—\n“(1)\n seek to ensure that any fund or mechanism established consistent with subsection (a) operates in accordance with established international accounting principles;\n“(2)\n seek to ensure that any fund or mechanism established consistent with subsection (a) is—\n“(A)\n staffed, operated, and administered in accordance with established accounting rules and governance procedures, including providing for payment of reasonable expenses from the fund for the governance and operation of the fund and the tribunal;\n“(B)\n operated transparently as to all funds transfers, filings, and decisions; and\n“(C)\n audited on a regular basis by an independent auditor, in accordance with internationally accepted accounting and auditing standards;\n“(3)\n seek to ensure that any audits of any fund or mechanism established consistent with subsection (a) shall be made available to the public; and\n“(4)\n ensure that any audits of any fund or mechanism established consistent with subsection (a) shall be reviewed and reported on by the Government Accountability Office to the appropriate congressional committees and the public.\n“(e)\n Limitation on Transfer of Funds.—\nNo funds may be transferred from the Ukraine Support Fund to a fund or mechanism established consistent with subsection (a) unless the President certifies to the appropriate congressional committees that—\n“(1)\n the institution housing the fund or mechanism has a plan to ensure transparency and accountability for all funds transferred to and from the fund or mechanism established consistent with subsection (a); and\n“(2)\n the President has transmitted the plan required under paragraph (1) to the appropriate congressional committees in writing.\n“(f)\n Joint Resolution of Disapproval.—\nNo funds may be transferred from the Ukraine Support Fund to a fund or mechanism established consistent with subsection (a) if, within 30 days of receipt of the notification required under subsection (c)(2) [probably should be “subsection (c)”], a joint resolution is enacted prohibiting the transfer.\n“(g)\n Report.—\nNot later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this division [Apr. 24, 2024], and not less frequently than every 90 days thereafter, the President shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees a report that includes the following:\n“(1)\n An accounting of funds in any fund or mechanism established consistent with subsection (a).\n“(2)\n Any information regarding the disposition of any such fund or mechanism that has been transmitted to the President by the institution housing the fund or mechanism during the period covered by the report.\n“(3)\n A description of United States multilateral and bilateral diplomatic engagement with allies and partners of the United States that also have immobilized Russian sovereign assets to allow for compensation for Ukraine during the period covered by the report.\n“(4)\n An outline of steps taken to carry out this section during the period covered by the report.\n“SEC. 106.\n REPORT ON USE OF TRANSFERRED RUSSIAN SOVEREIGN ASSETS FOR RECONSTRUCTION.\n“Not later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this division [Apr. 24, 2024], and every 180 days thereafter, the Secretary of State, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees a report that contains—\n“(1)\n the amount and source of Russian sovereign assets seized, transferred, or confiscated pursuant to section 104(b);\n“(2)\n the amount and source of funds deposited into the Ukraine Support Fund under section 104(b)(3); and\n“(3)\n a detailed description and accounting of how such funds were used to meet the purposes described in section 104(f).\n“SEC. 107.\n ASSESSMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE AND ADMINISTRATOR OF USAID ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REBUILDING NEEDS OF UKRAINE.\n“(a)\n In General.—\nNot later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this division [Apr. 24, 2024], the Secretary of State, in consultation with the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development, shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees an assessment of the most pressing needs of Ukraine for reconstruction, rebuilding, and humanitarian aid.\n“(b)\n Elements.—\nThe assessment required by subsection (a) shall include the following:\n“(1)\n An estimate of the rebuilding and reconstruction needs of Ukraine, as of the date of the assessment, resulting from the unlawful invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation, including—\n“(A)\n a description of the sources and methods for the estimate; and\n“(B)\n an identification of the locations or regions in Ukraine with the most pressing needs.\n“(2)\n An estimate of the humanitarian needs, as of the date of the assessment, of the people of Ukraine, including Ukrainians residing inside the internationally recognized borders of Ukraine or outside those borders, resulting from the unlawful invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation.\n“(3)\n An assessment of the extent to which the needs described in paragraphs (1) and (2) have been met or funded, by any source, as of the date of the assessment.\n“(4)\n A plan to engage in robust multilateral and bilateral diplomacy to ensure that allies and partners of the United States, particularly in the European Union as Ukraine seeks accession to the European Union, increase their commitment to Ukraine’s reconstruction.\n“(5)\n An identification of which such needs should be prioritized, including any assessment or request by the Government of Ukraine with respect to the prioritization of such needs.\n“SEC. 108.\n EXTENSIONS.\n“[Amended section 5(a) of Pub. L. 115–441, 132 Stat. 5587.]”\nImposition of Sanctions With Respect to the Sale, Supply, or Transfer of Gold to or From Russia\nPub. L. 117–263, div. E, title LV, § 5590, Dec. 23, 2022, 136 Stat. 3380, provided that:\n“(a)\n Identification.—\nNot later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this Act [Dec. 23, 2022], and periodically as necessary thereafter, the President—\n“(1)\n shall submit to Congress a report identifying foreign persons that knowingly participated in a significant transaction—\n“(A)\n for the sale, supply, or transfer (including transportation) of gold, directly or indirectly, to or from the Russian Federation or the Government of the Russian Federation, including from reserves of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation held outside the Russian Federation; or\n“(B)\n that otherwise involved gold in which the Government of the Russian Federation had any interest; and\n“(2)\n shall impose the sanctions described in subsection (b)(1) with respect to each such person; and\n“(3)\n may impose the sanctions described in subsection (b)(2) with respect to any such person that is an alien.\n“(b)\n Sanctions Described.—\nThe sanctions described in this subsection are the following:\n“(1)\n Blocking of property.—\nThe exercise of all powers granted to the President by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) to the extent necessary to block and prohibit all transactions in all property and interests in property of a foreign person identified in the report required by subsection (a)(1) if such property and interests in property are in the United States, come within the United States, or are or come within the possession or control of a United States person.\n“(2)\n Ineligibility for visas, admission, or parole.—\n“(A)\n Visas, admission, or parole.—\nAn alien described in subsection (a)(1) is—\n“(i)\n inadmissible to the United States;\n“(ii)\n ineligible to receive a visa or other documentation to enter the United States; and\n“(iii)\n otherwise ineligible to be admitted or paroled into the United States or to receive any other benefit under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.).\n“(B)\n Current visas revoked.—\n“(i)\n In general.—\nThe issuing consular officer, the Secretary of State, or the Secretary of Homeland Security (or a designee of one of such Secretaries) shall, in accordance with section 221(i) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1201(i)), revoke any visa or other entry documentation issued to an alien described in subsection (a)(1).\n“(ii)\n Immediate effect.—\nThe revocation under clause (i) of a visa or other entry documentation issued to an alien shall—\n     “(I)\n take effect immediately; and\n     “(II)\n automatically cancel any other valid visa or entry documentation that is in the alien’s possession.\n“(c)\n Implementation; Penalties.—\n“(1)\n Implementation.—\nThe President may exercise all authorities provided under sections 203 and 205 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1702 and 1704) to carry out this section.\n“(2)\n Penalties.—\nA person that violates, attempts to violate, conspires to violate, or causes a violation of this section or any regulation, license, or order issued to carry out this section shall be subject to the penalties set forth in subsections (b) and (c) of section 206 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1705) to the same extent as a person that commits an unlawful act described in subsection (a) of that section.\n“(d)\n National Interest Waiver.—\nThe President may waive the imposition of sanctions under this section with respect to a person if the President—\n“(1)\n determines that such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States; and\n“(2)\n submits to Congress a notification of the waiver and the reasons for the waiver.\n“(e)\n Termination.—\n“(1)\n In general.—\nExcept as provided in paragraph (2), the requirement to impose sanctions under this section, and any sanctions imposed under this section, shall terminate on the earlier of—\n“(A)\n the date that is 3 years after the date of the enactment of this Act; or\n“(B)\n the date that is 30 days after the date on which the President certifies to Congress that—\n“(i)\n the Government of the Russian Federation has ceased its destabilizing activities with respect to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine; and\n“(ii)\n such termination in the national interests of the United States.\n“(2)\n Transition rules.—\n“(A)\n Continuation of certain authorities.—\nAny authorities exercised before the termination date under paragraph (1) to impose sanctions with respect to a foreign person under this section may continue to be exercised on and after that date if the President determines that the continuation of those authorities is in the national interests of the United States.\n“(B)\n Application to ongoing investigations.—\nThe termination date under paragraph (1) shall not apply to any investigation of a civil or criminal violation of this section or any regulation, license, or order issued to carry out this section, or the imposition of a civil or criminal penalty for such a violation, if—\n“(i)\n the violation occurred before the termination date; or\n“(ii)\n the person involved in the violation continues to be subject to sanctions pursuant to subparagraph (A).\n“(f)\n Exceptions.—\n“(1)\n Exceptions for authorized intelligence and law enforcement and national security activities.—\nThis section shall not apply with respect to activities subject to the reporting requirements under title V of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 3091 et seq.) or any authorized intelligence, law enforcement, or national security activities of the United States.\n“(2)\n Exception to comply with international agreements.—\nSanctions under subsection (b)(2) may not apply with respect to the admission of an alien to the United States if such admission is necessary to comply with the obligations of the United States under the Agreement regarding the Headquarters of the United Nations, signed at Lake Success June 26, 1947, and entered into force November 21, 1947, between the United Nations and the United States, or the Convention on Consular Relations, done at Vienna April 24, 1963, and entered into force March 19, 1967, or other international obligations.\n“(3)\n Humanitarian exemption.—\nThe President shall not impose sanctions under this section with respect to any person for conducting or facilitating a transaction for the sale of agricultural commodities, food, medicine, or medical devices or for the provision of humanitarian assistance.\n“(4)\n Exception relating to importation of goods.—\n“(A)\n In general.—\nThe requirement or authority to impose sanctions under this section shall not include the authority or a requirement to impose sanctions on the importation of goods.\n“(B)\n Good defined.—\nIn this paragraph, the term ‘good’ means any article, natural or manmade substance, material, supply, or manufactured product, including inspection and test equipment, and excluding technical data.\n“(g)\n Definitions.—\nIn this section:\n“(1)\n The terms ‘admission’, ‘admitted’, ‘alien’, and ‘lawfully admitted for permanent residence’ have the meanings given those terms in section 101 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101).\n“(2)\n The term ‘foreign person’ means an individual or entity that is not a United States person.\n“(3)\n The term ‘knowingly’, with respect to conduct, a circumstance, or a result, means that a person has actual knowledge, or should have known, of the conduct, the circumstance, or the result.\n“(4)\n The term ‘United States person’ means—\n“(A)\n a United States citizen or an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence to the United States;\n“(B)\n an entity organized under the laws of the United States or any jurisdiction within the United States, including a foreign branch of such an entity; or\n“(C)\n any person in the United States.”\nExecutive Documents\nEx. Ord. No. 13849. Authorizing the Implementation of Certain Sanctions Set Forth in the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act\nEx. Ord. No. 13849, Sept. 20, 2018, 83 F.R. 48195, provided:\nBy the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, including the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.), the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (Public Law 115–44) (CAATSA), the Ukraine Freedom Support Act of 2014 (Public Law 113–272), as amended [22 U.S.C. 8921 et seq.] (UFSA), section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 (8 U.S.C. 1182(f)), and section 301 of title 3, United States Code,\nI, DONALD J. Executive Order 13757 of December 28, 2016 (Taking \nVerDate Sep<11>2014 23:02 Oct 31, 2023 Jkt 262001 PO 00000 Frm 00009 Fmt 4705 Sfmt 4790 E:\\FR\\FM\\01NOE0.SGM 01NOE0ddrumheller on DSK120RN23PROD Respect to Signifi-\ncant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities), and further amended by Executive \nOrder 13984, to address the use of United States Infrastructure as a Service \n(IaaS) Products by wording lead; chronology does not decide legal effect.","provision_text":"Section 1. Policy. It is the policy of the United States to restrict access \nby countries of concern to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and \nUnited States Government-related data when such access would pose an \nunacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. At the same \ntime, the United States continues to support open, global, interoperable, \nreliable, and secure flows of data across borders, as well as maintaining \nvital consumer, economic, scientific, and trade relationships that the United \nStates has with other countries. \nThe continuing effort by countries of concern to access Americans’ bulk \nsensitive personal data and United States Government-related data threatens \nthe national security and foreign policy of the United States. Such countries’ \ngovernments may seek to access and use sensitive personal data in a manner \nVerDate Sep<11>2014 22:57 Feb 29, 2024 Jkt 262001 PO 00000 Frm 00003 Fmt 4705 Sfmt 4790 E:\\FR\\FM\\01MRE0.SGM 01MRE0ddrumheller on DSK120RN23PROD with PRESDOC-E0\n=== PDF page 2 of 10 ===\n15422 Federal Register / Vol. 89, No. 42 / Friday, March 1, 2024 / Presidential Documents \nthat is not in accordance with democratic values, safeguards for privacy, \nand other human rights and freedoms. Such countries’ approach stands \nin sharp contrast to the practices of democracies with respect to sensitive \npersonal data and principles reflected in the Organisation for Economic \nCo-operation and Development Declaration on Government Access to Per-\nsonal Data Held by Private Sector Entities. Unrestricted transfers of Ameri-\ncans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related \ndata to such countries of concern may therefore enable them to exploit \nsuch data for a variety of nefarious purposes, including to engage in malicious \ncyber-enabled activities. Countries of concern can use their access to Ameri-\ncans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related \ndata to track and build profiles on United States individuals, including \nFederal employees and contractors, for illicit purposes, including blackmail \nand espionage. Access to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United \nStates Government-related data by countries of concern through data \nbrokerages, third-party vendor agreements, employment agreements, invest-\nment agreements, or other such arrangements poses particular and unaccept-\nable risks to our national security given that these arrangements often can \nprovide countries of concern with direct and unfettered access to Americans’ \nbulk sensitive personal data. Countries of concern can use access to United \nStates persons’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government- \nrelated data to collect information on activists, academics, journalists, dis-\nsidents, political figures, or members of non-governmental organizations or \nmarginalized communities in order to intimidate such persons; curb dissent \nor political opposition; otherwise limit freedoms of expression, peaceful \nassembly, or association; or enable other forms of suppression of civil lib-\nerties. \nThis risk of access to Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United \nStates Government-related data is not limited to direct access by countries \nof concern. Entities owned by, and entities or individuals controlled by \nor subject to the jurisdiction or direction of, a country of concern may \nenable the government of a country of concern to indirectly access such \ndata. For example, a country of concern may have cyber, national security, \nor intelligence laws that, without sufficient legal safeguards, obligate such \nentities and individuals to provide that country’s intelligence services access \nto Americans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government- \nrelated data. \nThese risks may be exacerbated when countries of concern use bulk sensitive \npersonal data to develop AI capabilities and algorithms that, in turn, enable \nthe use of large datasets in increasingly sophisticated and effective ways \nto the detriment of United States national security. Countries of concern \ncan use AI to target United States persons for espionage or blackmail by, \nfor example, recognizing patterns across multiple unrelated datasets to iden-\ntify potential individuals whose links to the Federal Government would \nbe otherwise obscured in a single dataset. \nWhile aspects of this threat have been addressed in previous executive \nactions, such as Executive Order 13694 of April 1, 2015 (Blocking the \nProperty of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled \nActivities), as amended, additional steps need to be taken to address this \nthreat. \nAt the same time, the United States is committed to promoting an open, \nglobal, interoperable, reliable, and secure Internet; protecting human rights \nonline and offline; supporting a vibrant, global economy by promoting cross- \nborder data flows required to enable international commerce and trade; \nand facilitating open investment. To ensure that the United States continues \nto meet these important policy objectives, this order does not authorize \nthe imposition of generalized data localization requirements to store Ameri-\ncans’ bulk sensitive personal data or United States Government-related data \nwithin the United States or to locate computing facilities used to process \nAmericans’ bulk sensitive personal data or United States Government-related \nVerDate Sep<11>2014 22:57 Feb 29, 2024 Jkt 262001 PO 00000 Frm 00004 Fmt 4705 Sfmt 4790 E:\\FR\\FM\\01MRE0.SGM 01MRE0ddrumheller on DSK120RN23PROD with PRESDOC-E0\n=== PDF page 3 of 10 ===\n15423 Federal Register / Vol. 89, No. 42 / Friday, March 1, 2024 / Presidential Documents \ndata within the United States. This order also does not broadly prohibit \nUnited States persons from conducting commercial transactions, including \nexchanging financial and other data as part of the sale of commercial goods \nand services, with entities and individuals located in or subject to the \ncontrol, direction, or jurisdiction of countries of concern, or impose measures \naimed at a broader decoupling of the substantial consumer, economic, sci-\nentific, and trade relationships that the United States has with other countries. \nIn addition, my Administration has made commitments to increase public \naccess to the results of taxpayer-funded scientific research, the sharing and \ninteroperability of electronic health information, and patient access to their \ndata. The national security restrictions established in this order are specific, \ncarefully calibrated actions to minimize the risks associated with access \nto bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data \nby countries of concern while minimizing disruption to commercial activity. \nThis order shall be implemented consistent with these policy objectives, \nincluding by tailoring any regulations issued and actions taken pursuant \nto this order to address the national security threat posed by access to \nAmericans’ bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government- \nrelated data by countries of concern.","sections_touched":["Section 1"],"signing_date":"2024-02-28","source":{"filing_date":null,"location_confidence":"high","location_verified":false,"page_or_item":"89 FR 15421, PDF pages 1-10","requires_page_check":false,"sha256":"ba21fdd74728be89271083248554b507b06e314bfcffba02554b1f08f3dadb9c","signing_date":"2024-02-28","text_path":"jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_14117.txt","text_sha256":"356519c03acd1192515d84aeeca3ecd6f4861b40b160c2ad37d51718cfe9ed38","url":"https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-03-01/pdf/2024-04573.pdf"},"verb":"transfer"},{"actor_id":"EO:14144","char_end":54345,"char_start":53225,"confidence":"medium","how_named":"parent_as_amended","id":"CHAIN:EO:13757#5","notes":"Change wording lead; chronology does not decide legal effect.","provision_text":"Because I find that additional steps must be taken to deal with \nthe national emergency with respect to significant malicious cyber-enabled \nactivities declared in Executive Order 13694 of April 1, 2015 (Blocking \nthe Property of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber- \nEnabled Activities), as amended by Executive Order 13757 of December \n28, 2016 (Taking Additional Steps to Address the National Emergency With \nRespect to Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities), and further \namended by Executive Order 13984 of January 19, 2021 (Taking Additional \nSteps to Address the National Emergency With Respect to Significant Mali-\ncious Cyber-Enabled Activities), to protect against the growing and evolving \nthreat of malicious cyber-enabled activities against the United States and \nUnited States allies and partners, including the increasing threats by foreign \nactors of unauthorized access to critical infrastructure, ransomware, and \ncyber-enabled intrusions and sanctions evasion, I hereby order that section \n1(a) of Executive Order 13694 is further amended to read as follows: \n‘‘Section 1.","sections_touched":["section \n1(a)","Section 1"],"signing_date":"2025-01-16","source":{"filing_date":null,"location_confidence":"high","location_verified":false,"page_or_item":"90 FR 6755, PDF pages 1-17","requires_page_check":false,"sha256":"006cddd54c6f3aeb42eb0ca48b36a692c13ad47d01c91ad47e7e07a99c82691d","signing_date":"2025-01-16","text_path":"jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_14144.txt","text_sha256":"7aca76eea4b17e70b4cfa07706df3f6c544da4fc1f58c5cbee8917441f3bcd8b","url":"https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-17/pdf/2025-01470.pdf"},"verb":"amend"}],"generic_refs_excluded":234,"id":"CHAIN:EO:13757","notes":"Named, located change provisions only;
